content.thinking:
Since evidence is sparse, I should keep claims minimal — the only solid fact is that alert AL1 fired for error rate above threshold, so I'll state the symptom as "io-shop returned errors to requests" sourced directly to AL1, rather than assuming what users experienced.

Beyond that, I can't trace a cause: metrics, logs, and pod data are all empty, and there's no change or flag flip in the window (T16 shows flags unchanged). Since no step ties the incident to a specific change, I won't force a ruled_out entry anywhere — I'll keep this as a single symptom step without fabricating causal links.

I'm also noting contributing factors: nobody was paged despite the alert, telemetry for io-shop was unreadable (zero metrics, zero logs, no pods reported), and the deployment history doesn't even name the revision currently running — the change-event feed came back empty too. These gaps compound each other and would have slowed any investigation regardless of root cause.

For action items, I'm drafting: route HighErrorRate alerts on io-shop to on-call paging, investigate why the metrics and log queries returned nothing, resolve the conflict between platform reporting no pods while deployment shows three replicas running, and start recording revision names in deployment history. I'm also considering whether pulling error data from the downstream dependencies (io-pricing, io-summary-cache, io-pay) counts as a valid investigative action item since root cause isn't confirmed yet.

For lessons learned, I'm noting Argus escalated on insufficient evidence rather than guessing as a positive, while leaving went_wrong and got_lucky mostly empty since nothing clearly qualifies as a contributing factor. For still_at_risk, the key point is that whatever caused the error rate spike was never identified, so io-shop remains vulnerable to recurrence.

For assumptions, I'm being careful to reference placeholders like {rule_waits} and {T12.2} instead of hardcoding specific numbers like "5m" or "three replicas." For the symptom line, I'm keeping it short and focused on the actual user-facing failure — something like "io-shop returned errors to requests."

action_items.item: Link the HighErrorRate alert on io-shop to an on-call rotation so that a person is paged when it fires.
Find out why the per-minute metrics query for io-shop returned no data, and fix it so Argus can read the service's error rate.
Find out why the log query for io-shop returned no log lines, and fix log collection or the query.
Work out why the platform reported no pods for io-shop while the deployment showed replicas running a revision, and fix whichever of the two readings is wrong.
Make the io-shop deployment history record the name of each revision it rolls out, and send deploys and releases to the change-event feed Argus reads.
Get error data for this period from the dependencies io-pricing, io-summary-cache and io-pay (from checkout-platform and IO Payments Ltd) to establish whether one of them caused the errors.

causal_chain.step: Requests to io-shop failed with errors. The alert fired because the error rate stayed above its threshold for {rule_waits}. The rate itself was never measured: Argus read back {T5.2} minutes of metrics and {T9.2} log lines. The record does not show why the errors happened. No production change came back ({T11.2} changes), and the deployment history does not name the revision running on the replicas. The evidence stops here.

contributing_factors.factor: No on-call incident was linked to the HighErrorRate alert on io-shop, so nobody was paged when it fired.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: A person would have been working on the incident from the moment the alert fired. They could have looked at the service and its dependencies directly when Argus found no evidence, instead of the incident waiting for the escalation to be picked up.
contributing_factors.label: CF-1

contributing_factors.factor: Argus could not get usable telemetry for io-shop: the metrics query returned {T5.2} minutes, the log query returned {T9.2} lines, and the platform reported no pods, even though the deployment read showed {T12.2} replicas running one revision.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: Argus could have measured the error rate, dated when the errors began and read the failing requests' log lines. That might have identified a cause and an action, instead of escalating for lack of evidence.
contributing_factors.label: CF-2

contributing_factors.factor: The deployment history does not name the revision the replicas run, and the change-event query returned no changes. So nothing in the record shows what is deployed or when it last changed.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: A recent change to io-shop could have been confirmed or ruled out as the trigger, which would have narrowed the investigation or pointed to a rollback.
contributing_factors.label: CF-3

went_well: Argus searched every evidence channel it had: metrics, logs, pods, production changes, deployment rollout, the service register and the flag provider's history.
When the evidence could not support a cause, Argus escalated the incident, {T17.1 - alert_raised} after the alert was raised, instead of acting on a guess.

input.still_at_risk: Nobody found or fixed whatever was causing io-shop's errors, so it could go on failing requests, or fail the same way again, while nobody was paged and Argus could not read the service's metrics or logs.
